title: Development and experimental characterization of aluminum oxide/epoxy composite for light duty brake pad application
abstract: In this work, asbestos-free brake pad composite has been developed using aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃), calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), graphite, and epoxy resin constituent materials. Twenty-seven specimens were fabricated using hot compression moulding following a Taguchi orthogonal array design. The composite properties were optimized using grey relation analysis (GRA) and response surface methodology (RSM) by considering curing temperature and time as processing parameters. The optimal formulations of 37% Al₂O₃, 25.2% CaCO₃, 26.8% epoxy, and 11% graphite cured at 148.7 °C for 6 h achieved compressive strength of 156.77 MPa, hardness of 128.2 HB, wear rate of 3.74 mg/m, thermal conductivity of 1.18 W/m·K, water absorption of 0.64%, and oil absorption of 0.33%. These values exceeded the commercial asbestos-based brake pad performance by 42.5% of compressive strength, 26.9% of hardness, 118.7% of thermal conductivity, and 28.9% of water resistance. The developed composite shows significant improvement for environmental friendly and high-performance applications compared to the asbestos-based brake pads.

title: Influence of Transversely-Isotropic Lining Elastic Constants on Brake Squeal in S-Cam Drum Brakes: An Optimization Framework
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: Brake squeal in heavy-duty S-cam drum brakes remains a persistent NVH challenge, primarily driven by friction-induced modal instabilities. Existing studies on drum brake squeal mitigation largely emphasize geometric modifications, stiffness tuning, or the application of damping treatments, while the influence of directional stiffness characteristics of friction linings remains insufficiently explored. This research presents a novel, material-centric approach by modelling the brake lining as a transversely isotropic material, characterized by six independent elastic constants, and systematically quantifying their influence on squeal-prone unstable modes using Complex Eigenvalue Analysis (CEA). A validated finite-element model of a production S-cam drum brake assembly is developed and correlated through experimental modal analysis, ensuring close agreement between predicted and measured natural frequencies and mode shapes. The validated model is then integrated with a Design of Experiments (DOE) within commercially available FEA software to quantify both main effects and higher-order interactions across practical ranges of in-plane and out-of-plane elastic moduli and shear constants. To enhance the predictive accuracy of the surrogate models, a subsequent sampling–fit study is conducted, significantly improving the coefficient of determination (R2) of the response surfaces. The refined surrogate models are employed within a Global Response Surface Methodology (GRSM) framework t

title: Multi-objective evaluation of friction drilling characteristics using Taguchi design and ANOVA
abstract: Friction drilling is a non-conventional technique that utilizes the heat generated by a rotating tool to penetrate material, simultaneously forming a bushing around the hole. In this study, the influence of key process parameters like spindle speed, feed rate, and material thickness on multiple output responses, including thrust force, torque, bush length, cylindricity, top diameter, and temperature, was systematically investigated using Taguchi optimization technique and analysis of variance (ANOVA). The results revealed that spindle speed was the most influential factor for thermal and force-related responses, particularly temperature and thrust force, where increasing speed from 2000 rpm to 5000 rpm reduced thrust force by nearly 22% (from ~ 1500 N to ~ 1170 N) and peak drilling temperature by about 15%. Feed rate played a secondary role, contributing significantly when coupled with spindle speed, especially in torque and bush length formation, where higher feeds (65 mm/min) increased torque by nearly 18% compared to the lowest feed setting. Material thickness exhibited a strong effect on thrust force and cylindricity, with thrust peaking at 3 mm thickness (~ 1600 N) before dropping at 4 mm (~ 1200 N), reflecting nonlinear deformation resistance. Two-way interactions, notably speed–thickness and speed–feed, dominated in responses such as torque, cylindricity, and top diameter, contributing more than 40% of total variance. Residual plots confirmed the adequacy of the ANOVA

title: Cultural Representations and Potential Intercultural Friction in the Tendance A1 Textbook: Implications for Beginner Indonesian Learners
journal: Journal of General Education and Humanities
abstract: Foreign language textbooks function not only as linguistic resources but also as vehicles for cultural transmission. In French as a Foreign Language (FLE) education, cultural representations embedded in teaching materials may generate intercultural tensions when they differ from learners’ sociocultural norms. Despite extensive research on culture in FLE textbooks, the potential for intercultural friction in beginner-level materials remains underexplored, particularly in the Indonesian context. This study aims to identify French cultural representations in the audiovisual content of the Tendance A1 textbook and examine their potential for intercultural friction from the perspective of Indonesian cultural values. Using an interpretive qualitative design, the study employs content analysis of audiovisual materials from Units 0 to 9. The analysis is informed by intercultural and ecolinguistic perspectives and focuses exclusively on textbook content rather than learners’ perceptions or experiences. The findings reveal four recurring domains of cultural representation: greeting practices involving la bise and physical contact, norms of intimacy and interpersonal distance, diverse family and romantic relationship models, and individual autonomy in everyday life. These representations reflect values of informality, personal freedom, and relational openness that may contrast with the more collective, family-oriented, and religiously influenced norms commonly associated with Indonesian

title: Effect of Friction Stir Additive Manufacturing on the Mechanical and Microstructural Properties of AISI 304 Stainless Steel
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The present work focuses on studying the effect of Friction Stir Additive Manufacturing on the mechanical and microstructural properties of AISI 304 stainless steel. AISI 304 stainless steel is widely used in structural, automotive, marine, aerospace, and chemical industries due to its formability, and mechanical strength. However, processing stainless steel through FSAM requires careful control of process parameters because of its relatively high melting point, high strength, and complex thermo-mechanical behavior during deformation. This report highlights the working principle of FSAM, its influence on material behavior, and the research progress reported by various authors using FSAM as a fabrication technique. The study also emphasizes the changes in hardness, corrosion behavior, and microstructure of AISI 304 stainless steel after FSAM processing. Optical microscopy is used to examine microstructural evolution, while hardness testing is performed to evaluate the mechanical and surface degradation behavior of the fabricated material.

title: Effects of Coulomb friction, gravity, and magnetoelastic coupling on Rayleigh waves in a reinforced layered composite structure
abstract: Rayleigh-type waves are highly sensitive to the mechanical and interfacial properties of layered media, making their study important for characterizing composite structures and geophysical materials. The present paper investigates the characteristics of Rayleigh wave propagation in a magnetoelastic fibre-reinforced layer overlying a pre-stressed magnetoelastic fibre-reinforced orthotropic half-space under gravity. The main contribution of this study is the development of a unified analytical framework that simultaneously incorporates magnetoelasticity, fibre reinforcement, orthotropy, initial stress, gravity, and a Coulomb-friction interface. An analytical approach, the method of separation of variables, is used to obtain displacement fields, and the corresponding dispersion relation is derived using appropriate boundary conditions. Some limiting cases are also discussed to recover the classical Rayleigh wave equation and to validate the proposed formulation. Numerical results computed in MATLAB using parameter values from the existing literature illustrate that the Rayleigh wave phase velocity is significantly affected by the initial stress, gravity, electromagnetic and magnetoelastic parameters, fibre-reinforcement parameters, and interfacial bonding conditions. The results show that interfacial friction plays a significant role in modifying Rayleigh wave characteristics, emphasizing the importance of imperfect interface modelling in layered composite and geophysical media.

title: Exploration of friction stir welding butted thin sheet NiTi with AA6061, AA2024, and AA7075
abstract: Friction stir welding was investigated as a method for producing dissimilar butt joints of 1-mm-thick NiTi sheet with three aluminum alloys: AA6061-T6, AA2024-T3, and AA7075-T6. Dissimilar welding of these materials could enable structural integration of shape memory alloys with common aerospace aluminum alloys, but differences in thermal and mechanical behavior make joining difficult. Joining NiTi and AA6061 was successful, while NiTi and AA2024 showed mixed results under tested conditions. NiTi and AA7075 did not join under tested conditions. Difficulty in joining AA2024 and AA7075 came from post-weld cracking attributed to residual stresses and thermal strain due to mismatch in coefficients of thermal expansion combined with lower ductility in the higher-strength aluminum alloys. Tensile testing showed that AA6061–NiTi welds retained moderate strength, with an average ultimate tensile strength of 167.8 MPa and a weld efficiency of 57.9% relative to AA6061-T6, while AA2024–NiTi welds showed lower strength and ductility, with an average tensile strength of 120 MPa and a weld efficiency of 27.6%. Fracture behavior suggests that failure was controlled by the ability of the interface to bear load across the joint. Microscopy revealed a region of dispersed NiTi particles in both AA6061 and AA2024 stir zones. Larger particles showed evidence of aluminum diffusion, while smaller particles were enriched in either Ni or Ti, consistent with formation of Ni-Al and Ti-Al intermetallic

title: Okra Biomass-Derived Pectin-Rich Polysaccharide Composite Coating for Formulation-Dependent Surface Friction on Mango Fruit
abstract: Valorisation of agro-industrial biomass into functional coatings offers a sustainable approach to developing bio-based materials for postharvest applications. Although polysaccharide–lipid coatings are widely studied for their barrier properties, their effects on fruit–packaging friction remain poorly understood. This study recovered pectin-rich polysaccharides (OP) from okra-processing biomass and developed OP–beeswax (BW) composite coatings to modify mango–packaging friction and evaluate selected postharvest quality attributes. Conventional thermal extraction (CTE) and microwave-assisted extraction (MAE) yielded OP with comparable degrees of esterification but distinct hydration properties, with extraction yields of 4.28% and 5.47%, respectively (p > 0.05). The recovered OP exhibited low-methoxyl characteristics, with a degree of esterification of approximately 47%. Film optical and microstructural properties varied with OP and BW levels. Coating performance was evaluated on three independent mango fruits per treatment (n = 3; 21 fruits in total), with the same fruits used for friction and all quality measurements. Static and kinetic coefficients of friction (COFs) at the mango–corrugated plastic board interface were in the ranges of 0.45–0.59 and 0.42–0.58, respectively, demonstrating formulation-dependent frictional behaviour. title: Experimental Investigation of Wheel–Rail Sliding Friction Coefficients under Varying Temperature and Humidity Conditions Using Innovative Testing Methods
journal: Transportation Research Record Journal of the Transportation Research Board
abstract: The sliding friction coefficient between wheel and rail materials plays a vital role in understanding creep and contact behavior in railway systems. This study investigates its variation under controlled temperature (5–45°C) and relative humidity (50%–80% RH) conditions. A novel experimental method was proposed to eliminate the influence of atmospheric pressure and account for additional adhesion caused by surface moisture under wet friction. A counterweight was also added to improve measurement stability. Results show that low temperature and high humidity promote water-film lubrication, significantly reducing the friction coefficient. Conversely, at high temperatures and humidity, oxidation and debris formation increase friction. The frictional response exhibits clear temperature-dependent transitions, which were visualized using heatmaps and modeled via surface fitting with relatively high correlation. These findings offer both mechanistic insights and predictive tools for understanding and managing wheel–rail contact behavior under varying climatic conditions, supporting more reliable design and maintenance strategies in high-speed railway operations.

title: Thickness Optimization of Constrained Layer Damping Shims for Reducing Friction-Induced Instabilities in Drum Brakes
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: Commercial vehicles predominantly employ drum brakes because of their low cost, robustness, and simple construction. However, with the increasing push toward quieter powertrains, particularly in electric commercial vehicles, brake squeal has become a dominant noise source. The inherent complex and chaotic nature of brake squeal makes its prediction and suppression especially challenging. Traditional squeal mitigation strategies, such as modifying component mass and stiffness or using materials with higher native damping (e.g., cast iron), are inherently constrained in their capacity to mitigate instability. In such scenarios, constrained layer damping (CLD) shims have proven to be an additional, effective and practical solution in disc brakes, which is motivating growing interest in extending similar concepts to drum brake applications. A key challenge in adopting shims for drum brakes lies in identifying and achieving the required damping level necessary to suppress squeal while adhering to stringent packaging, manufacturability, and cost constraints of foundation brakes. Establishing a clear relationship between squeal propensity, noise intensity, and target damping is therefore essential. While past CLD studies discuss layer-thickness effects in generic structures and caliper brakes, no work applies thickness optimization to brake shims in a drum brake assembly. This paper presents a systematic and target-driven framework for the design of CLD shims for drum brake applicat

title: Recent Advances in Nanocomposite for Lightweight Automotive Materials: A Systematic Review
abstract: Vehicle weight reduction is one of the most effective strategies for lowering energy consumption and emissions in both internal combustion and electric vehicles. Nanocomposites have attracted attention because they can significantly improve material properties at very low reinforcement contents. This study maps recent research on nanocomposites for lightweight automotive materials through a systematic review of 88 Scopus-indexed research articles published between 2021 and 2026. The number of articles increased more than sevenfold, from 4 in 2021 to 30 in 2026, and 59.1% of them appeared in the last two years. Polymer matrix nanocomposites dominate the field (45 articles; 51.1%), followed by aluminum matrices (27; 30.7%) and magnesium matrices (11; 12.5%). Graphene and its derivatives, together with carbon nanotubes (CNTs), are the most frequently studied reinforcements, while stir casting and its variants remain the main fabrication route for metal matrices. Nanoscale reinforcement, typically at 0.25–3 wt% in polymers and 1.5–10 wt% in metals, was reported to increase tensile strength by approximately 14–54% and to reduce the coefficient of friction by up to approximately 38%. One life cycle study reported a 28% reduction in component weight compared with a glass fiber composite. title: Bone Drilling Simulation: Effects of Drill Bit Material on Bone Temperature
abstract: Bone drilling is a critical surgical procedure in orthopaedic, dental, and maxillofacial surgery, during which excessive bone temperature elevation at the tool-bone interface can cause thermal osteonecrosis (bone temperature > 47 °C). The subsequent effects compromise osseointegration and implant stability. Drill coating material could regulate both frictional heat dissipation and mechanical cutting resistance. However, the comparative thermomechanical performance of titanium nitride (TiN), titanium carbonitride (TiCN), titanium carbide (TiC), and diamond coatings across multiple simultaneous drilling responses has not been systematically quantified under designed experimental conditions. A Box-Behnken Design (BBD) comprising 60 finite element simulation runs (15 per coating block, 3 centre points per block) was employed to develop second-order response surface methodology (RSM) models for maximum bone temperature and thrust force. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) revealed that the quadratic model was highly significant (F = 137.79, p < 0.0001), with coating material (D) as the dominant factor (F = 497.40), followed by spindle speed (A, F = 702.67), feed rate (B, F = 412.86), and drill diameter (C, F = 177.92). All three coating-by-continuous-parameter interactions (AD, BD, CD) were insignificant (p > 0.19), which indicates that the thermal advantage of diamond over TiN reveals as a uniform absolute offset independent of continuous parameter levels. title: Supplementary materials, code and data for "Hydrodynamic Penalty of Biofouling on Fouling-Control Coatings for FRP Fishing Boats: Coating-Calibrated Fouling Kinetics, Boundary-Layer CFD and Cleaning Strategy
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Supplementary materials for an article submitted to Coatings (MDPI). The archive contains the supplementary document (Figures S1-S4, Tables S1-S2), MATLAB R2026a source code (Codes S1, S2, S4) and a Python port (Code S3) of a coating-calibrated biofouling, hull-friction and boundary-layer CFD model of a 15 m FRP fishing boat, the simulation results (Data S1 and Code S4 tables), the sea-water algal counts used for calibration (Table S2), and all figure files. See README.md for contents and reproduction steps.

title: Dispersion characteristics of SH waves in Piezo–viscoelastic structure with dual-uncoupled interface for energy harvesting
abstract: Purpose The transmission of shear-horizontal (SH) waves in piezoelectric–viscoelastic (PEV) composite media has gained great attention due to its potential usage in sensing technologies, energy harvesting and non-destructive evaluation. In this work, the impact of interfacial internal friction on the attenuation and dispersion properties of SH waves in a PEV composite structure is explored. Design/methodology/approach The interface between a viscoelastic (VE) half-space and a PEV layer is modeled using a dual-membrane arrangement made up of a PEV membrane and a VE membrane separated by a classical spring layer, which accounts for frictional energy dissipation at the interface. Analytical formulas are constructed to derive the governing dispersion relation of the coupled system. Findings Parametric studies are carried out to assess the impact of important material and interfacial factors, including density, elastic stiffness, dielectric constants, piezoelectric coefficients and interfacial friction, on wave dispersion and attenuation. Originality/value The results reveal that interfacial internal friction considerably alters wave propagation properties modifying phase velocity. These findings provide important insights for the design and optimization of PEV multilayer composites in wave-based sensing and energy harvesting applications.

title: Effect of Counter-Surface Texturing on the Tribological Behavior of Virgin and Glass-Filled Polytetrafluoroethylene During Sliding Against Grey Cast Iron
abstract: In this research study, effect of laser surface texturing on the tribological performance of composite of polytetrafluoroethylene with 25 wt.% glass fibre against grey cast iron. Dimples (50 µm diameter) were ablated on GCI with dimple pitches of 100 µm and 150 µm. Friction and wear tests were conducted on a pin-on-disc tribometer under ambient conditions. Specific wear rate of both PTFE and its composite generally decreased with increasing sliding distance for all GCI surfaces, whether textured or untextured. The coefficient of friction (COF) followed a similar trend for PTFE but increased for 25 wt.% glass fibre/PTFE on textured GCI surfaces. Compared to untextured GCI, PTFE exhibited a 14.2-16.7% reduction in COF and specific wear rate when sliding against GCI with a 150 µm dimple pitch. For 25 wt.% glass fibre/PTFE, LST increased friction but significantly reduced specific wear rate by 66.6-73.2%.Increasing the dimple pitch from 100 µm to 150 µm further decreased COF and wear. FESEM micrographs of textured GCI surfaces post-sliding against PTFE revealed polymer debris deposition, forming transfer films that contributed to friction and wear reduction. These findings highlight the potential of LST in enhancing the tribological performance of PTFE-based materials, particularly in optimizing wear resistance and friction control through surface texturing.

title: Tribological Behavior of Ti-6Al-4V Alloys Processed by Selective Laser Melting and Conventional Casting Process
journal: Journal of Innovations in Materials and Manufacturing Engineering
abstract: This work presents a detailed assessment of the microstructural features and tribological behaviour of Ti6Al4V alloy produced by conventional casting followed by rolling (CR) and selective laser melting (SLM). The two fabrication routes yield markedly different microstructures: the CR alloy develops a dualphase α + β microstructure, whereas the SLM alloy forms a fine martensitic α′ lath morphology with enhanced hardness. Tribological experiments performed under various loads and sliding speeds reveal clear distinctions in frictional response and wear characteristics. The CR samples exhibit deeper ploughing grooves, stronger oxidation effects, and higher coefficients of friction, indicating that abrasive and oxidationassisted wear dominate their surface degradation. In contrast, the SLM samples show shallower wear tracks, reduced friction, and improved resistance to material removal, with delamination and adhesive wear occurring only under more severe test conditions. The lower COF and diminished wear severity observed in the SLM alloy highlight the advantages of its refined microstructure in stabilizing interfacial contact and reducing frictional energy losses. Overall, the results confirm the superior tribological performance of SLMprocessed Ti6Al4V for applications demanding high wear resistance and structural reliability.

title: Three-Dimensional Particle Shape and Stress–Dilatancy Behavior of Carbonate and Silica Sands at Low Normal Stresses: A Direct Simple Shear Investigation
journal: Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering
abstract: Abstract This multiscale study investigates the influence of three-dimensional (3D) particle shape on the stress–dilatancy behavior of granular materials under low-stress simple shear conditions. High-resolution X-ray micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) was first used to quantify the particle shapes of 11 different sands, spanning silica, carbonate, and mixed compositions. The images with a reconstructed voxel size of 5.5 μm were segmented using a watershed-based algorithm, which isolated more than 10,000 grains per material. This enabled particle-level quantification of 3D shape descriptors for each sand. The analyzed particle-size distributions were validated against those measured from mechanical sieve analysis. In the second phase, direct simple shear tests were conducted on three selected materials, UWA superfine silica, ledge point, and glass beads, considering relative densities of 0.4 to 0.9 and normal pressures of 25 to 150 kPa. The results show that particle shape affects peak friction, excess friction, and dilation response, but the magnitude of this effect depends on density and normal stress. Particle-shape effects are strongest at lower density and lower normal stress, where particle rearrangement and dilation are more readily mobilized. As relative density or normal stress increases, the responses of the three materials converge, indicating that the mechanical response becomes less sensitive to particle shape. title: Similitude Framework for Scale Modelling of Dry-Stacked Interlocking Compressed Earth Block Walls
abstract: Interlocking compressed earth blocks (ICEBs) are machine-pressed soil blocks that stack together like toy bricks, without mortar. They offer a low-cost, low-carbon way to build houses in earthquake-prone regions. Laboratory testing of ICEB walls remains rare because full-size tests need large and costly equipment. Testing small models instead would solve this problem, but only if clear rules exist to make the small model behave like the real wall. Such rules, called similitude rules, do not yet exist for dry-stacked interlocking earthen walls, because these walls act through friction and interlocking between blocks rather than as one solid material. This paper derives the missing rules using dimensional analysis. Three ratios must be matched between model and prototype: the friction between block faces, the ratio of key strength to friction resistance, and the ratio of vertical load to block strength. The paper shows how to correct the reduced self-weight of a small model with added weights, how to correct for size effects, and how to press model blocks in 3D-printed moulds. A quarter-scale worked example based on published test data requires only a 37 kg added weight and one sixteenth of the lateral testing force.

title: Dry-Sliding and Seawater Tribological Response of W-and Y-Modified Fe₃Al-Based Alloys
abstract: Abstract Selecting Fe₃Al-based alloys for sliding applications requires an understanding of how tungsten (W) and yttrium (Y) additions affect wear under both dry and seawater conditions. Here, Fe–28Al–5Cr alloys containing 0.5, 1.0, or 1.5 at.% W, with or without 0.1 at.% Y, were produced by vacuum arc melting and evaluated by ball-on-disc testing against AISI 52100 steel at 5 N, 0.05 m s⁻¹, and sliding distances of 100–500 m. Wear volume, specific wear rate, friction, microhardness, and worn-surface evolution were examined by profilometry, optical microscopy, x-ray diffraction, and scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy. Fe–28Al–5Cr–0.5W–0.1Y provided the most favorable overall response in both environments, combining low wear with comparatively limited visible cracking and broader Al/O-rich coverage in the examined worn regions. Seawater reduced friction, while post-test surfaces showed heterogeneous O-rich regions and localized Cl, Na, and Mg signals. These observations describe an environment-dependent surface response; quantification of corrosion-related material loss requires electrochemical measurements and separate control tests. The results identify a favorable composition within the tested series, while the relative roles of bulk microstructure and tribo-oxide formation or retention in the Y-associated response remain unresolved.

title: Signal carriers and the structural logic of reassurance: a configurational account of escalation in East Asian security interactions
abstract: Why do some ostensibly ‘soft’ deterrence signals coincide with sharper escalation than sustained material pressure? Existing theories emphasise signal cost and credibility, yet East Asian interactions suggest that signal intensity and response severity do not always align. This article proposes a configurational framework linking signal carrier, structural reassurance and adversary cognition. It examines three Japan–China cases—the phased reinforcement of the Southwestern Islands, the 2014 reinterpretation of collective self-defense and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s November 2025 Diet remarks on a ‘survival-threatening situation’. The evidence suggests that signals preserving operational adjustability, observable conditions and institutional friction leave room for gain-domain monitoring and incremental response, whereas signals that narrow these channels are more likely to trigger loss-prevention or identity-defensive framing. The article thus extends reassurance scholarship by specifying how material, legal and institutional signal forms shape whether restraint appears capable of preserving a recoverable position.

title: CSI-008: La rampa del mistero
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A supply box must reach a raised shelf. A short, steep ramp and a longer, gentler ramp both lead to the same height. If the longer ramp requires less pulling force, does it also require less work? In this ERNEST Classroom Science Investigation for nursing students, groups compare a vertical lift with pulls along both ramps, keeping the load and vertical rise constant. They measure the applied force and the distance over which it acts, then compare the work done with the change in gravitational potential energy. Friction gives the comparison its investigative value: the same final height fixes the gain in potential energy, but does not guarantee that the applied force does the same amount of work along every route. The resource includes a student dossier and a teacher’s guide. Language of the teaching materials: Italian.

title: Comment on egusphere-2026-4035
abstract: Abstract. Sea ice is a quasi-brittle material that cracks, deforms, and flows under the load of wind and ocean currents. In part I we introduced QuSI-DEM, a model designed to capture crack patterns that develop as a result of sea ice fracture that depend critically on the elastic and dissipative response of the material at the location of failure. Parameters were introduced to the contact physics in QuSI-DEM to provide control of the failure rate and timing of transitions in contact response and to constrain the amount of energy and momentum transfer as elements interact. The sensitivity of the model response to these parameters is first demonstrated here in a set of idealized experiments involving the interactions of a few elements. The model is then applied to realistic simulations of sea ice response to northerly wind stress in the southern Chukchi Sea and Bering Strait. Here again, the parameter space is explored along with sensitivity to element size and arrangement through sets of ensemble simulations to explore the phenomenology of ice arching. Post-failure parameters such as the strength of the sea ice at the transition from bonded to frictional sliding, and the residual sea ice strength for heavily impacted ice are found to significantly impact model response.

title: Thermomechanical properties and high-temperature stability of epoxy resin modified with boron-based inorganic phases
journal: Journal of Thermal Analysis and Calorimetry
abstract: Abstract This study concerns the manufacturing and complex characterization of the Epidian 5 epoxy resin with the addition of low-density ceramic phases, containing boron in their crystallographic structure. The composite was designed to contain fine powders of boron carbide and hexagonal boron nitride in quantities up to 20 vol% as reference compositions, compared with a material prepared with up to 20 vol% of a 50/50 vol% mixture of boron carbide and boron nitride. Low additive contents caused a slight decrease in the glass transition temperature, whereas significant changes in storage modulus were observed at inorganic phase concentrations of 10 vol% and above. The incorporation of boron-based phases generally resulted in nearly linear changes in thermal transport properties and hardness. Hexagonal boron nitride exerted the strongest effect on thermal diffusivity and thermal conductivity, while boron carbide produced the most pronounced increase in hardness. Composites containing the BCBN mixture exhibited intermediate thermal and mechanical properties, particularly at higher inorganic phase concentrations. The paper explains material’s behavior through thermal analysis, dynamic mechanical analysis, dilatometry and heat transfer, and the correlations among them. Due to the wide range of potential applications, including military, electrical and coating technologies, the paper characterizes and analyzes the influence of boron-based phases and their mixtures of friction coef

title: Study on the high-temperature oxidative wear behaviors of Inconel 690 and Hastelloy N alloys in a simulated rotary calcination furnace environment
abstract: Given the important role of rotary calcination furnaces in the immobilization process of nuclear waste and the fact that few researches focused on the materials used inside the furnace, this paper studied the oxidative wear behaviors and mechanisms of Inconel 690 and Hastelloy N alloys at 600 and 800 ℃ by using a specially designed high-temperature friction and wear testing machine. The results reveal that Inconel 690 forms an oxide film characterized by a double-layer structure after wearing at 800 ℃. The continuous Cr 2 O 3 inner layer plays a crucial protective role for the substrate, which results in the better oxidative wear resistance for Inconel 690 at 800 ℃ than at 600 ℃. In contrast, the loose and porous Mo-O layers formed on the surface of Hastelloy N alloy after wearing at both 600 and 800 ℃ are responsible for its poorer oxidative wear resistance than Inconel 690 alloy.

title: On the Effect of Hydrogen on the Wear of the Rolling Surface of Railway Tires and a Method for Improving Its Hardness
abstract: Abstract The effect of free hydrogen released during the decomposition of lubricant due to friction on the stress state of the locomotive wheel set tire is studied. Analytical solution was obtained and the stress-strain state of a locomotive wheel with a railway tire pressed onto it was calculated. Under the influence of hydrogen, a weakened layer is shown to form in the band, leading to an increase in stresses in the near surface rolling zone, which negatively affects the wear resistance of the band. The issue of increasing the hardness of the band’s rolling surface to reduce the intensity of wear after mechanical turning is also studied. A method of hardening it by rolling on a special installation is proposed. A model of force loading of the locomotive wheel set bandage in the form of a cylindrical striker hitting the surface of the bandage being hardened is proposed. For this model, a system of second-order partial differential equations was derived using the Hamilton–Ostrogradsky variational principle whose solution determines the effective hardening limit of the wheel tire material.

title: What Is Actually Under Attack: Ground, Mediation, and the Real Vulnerability in Cognitive Warfare
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Cognitive warfare is usually studied as a contest over what populations believe. This working paper argues that the deeper target is ground: the prereflexive, taken-for-granted material from which a person or people argues rather than about which they argue. A signal lands only where ground exists for it to land on. The literature is rich on mechanisms of influence but underdeveloped on the standing condition that makes those mechanisms effective. The paper develops a conceptual architecture organised around mediation, ground, surfacing, and the capacity to hold unresolved states. It traces the attack through three layers ordered by depth: the familiar horizontal (nation-state) attack across borders; a transverse attack from the non-state mediating layer of platforms and systems that now stand between populations and reality on every side at once; and a temporal layer of structural substitution, in which systems that answer on demand progressively stand in for the judgment-forming work through which independent judgment is built across formative windows. Judgment is formed against friction. Removing that friction at scale may leave the precondition of holding unbuilt. This developmental claim is stated as a testable hypothesis. The paper is addressed to those responsible for Alliance resilience. title: Development of aluminum metal foam with improved mechanical properties through the novel FSP technique
journal: Advances in Materials and Processing Technologies
abstract: Aluminum 6063 metal foam with densities ranging from 0.885 to 1.5 g/cm3 was successfully formed using friction stir processing (FSP) method. To gain a fair control over the pore morphology, the relationship between FSP parameters and the resulting foam structure, as well as the mechanical properties, needs to be analysed. The effect of tool design parameters and the powder ratio of blowing and stabilizing agents on density and morphology was reported. A fractional factorial technique was used to optimize these factors, in order to interprettheir impact on the final foam structure. The approach led to high-quality metal foams with porosities ranging from 38.6% to 67.2%. The specific compressive strength and energy absorption capacity of 26.04 kNm/kg and 12 MJ/m3 respectively was observed for the foam with minimum relative density of 0.37. This study outlines that critical input parameters for producing the most efficient foam with the lowest density include ratio of blowing and stabilizing agents, traverse speed and spindle speed. Hence, it provides valuable insights for researchers working on the design and development of advanced foaming techniques aimed at controlling the essential physical properties of this important class of materials.

title: Crashworthiness and energy partitioning in monolithic and layered thin-walled metallic tubes under axial impact
abstract: This study numerically investigates the axial impact response of monolithic and layered circular and square-shaped mild steel and aluminium hollow tubes. Tubes of 200 mm length and three equivalent cross-sectional sizes were subjected to low-velocity impact by a 350-kg rigid mass. ABAQUS/Explicit simulations employed S4R shell elements, a strain-rate-dependent Johnson–Cook material model and a general contact interaction algorithm. Deformation and energy absorption in plastic, elastic, and frictional energy components were compared. Force–displacement histories were used to assess mean crushing force, specific energy absorption, and crushing force efficiency. Layered tubes showed increased axial deformation by up to 51.53% for circular sections and approximately 15% for square sections, depending on size. However, monolithic tubes exhibited slightly higher total energy absorption through predominantly plastic dissipation. Moreover, circular tubes demonstrated superior crashworthiness to square tubes, associated with stable deformation modes and more uniform stress distributions. The findings have explored layering-induced deformation and energy dissipation mechanisms.

title: Design and biomechanical evaluation of a patient-specific 3D-printed wrist splint for carpal tunnel syndrome: a finite element analysis study
journal: Computer Methods in Biomechanics & Biomedical Engineering
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Conventional wrist splints for carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) may have limited anatomical fit and ventilation. This study developed and mechanically evaluated an anatomy-matched, 3D-printed wrist splint using stress-guided Voronoi lattice optimisation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Wrist and forearm geometry from one healthy adult volunteer was acquired by structured-light scanning (0.2 mm point distance). A 3.0 mm shell was optimised by preserving longitudinal and transverse load-bearing features and removing material from low-strain regions. A coupled splint-soft-tissue finite element analysis (FEA) model with frictional contact (μ = 0.4) simulated a static 50 N wrist-flexion load. Global displacement predictions were assessed by mechanical bench testing of the printed polylactic acid (PLA) splint. A non-porous 3.0 mm solid shell derived from the same anatomy served as the design comparator. RESULTS: Under the simulated load, maximum von Mises stress was 18.4 MPa against a PLA yield strength of 60 MPa, with a minimum safety factor of 3.26. Predicted distal displacement was 2.15 mm, compared with 2.32 mm in bench testing (7.33% relative error). Compared with the solid-shell control, the optimised design reduced mass by 45.93% and achieved a 45.2% open surface area while retaining adequate static load-bearing capacity. CONCLUSIONS: This single-volunteer proof-of-concept study supports the feasibility of a lightweight, anatomy-matched splint with mechanically validated gl

title: Transmission mechanism and identification of power pulsation signals in sucker rod pumping wells
abstract: Abstract Traditional wellbore communication technologies for sucker-rod pumping wells suffer from severe signal attenuation and poor stability under deep-well and complex operating conditions. This study investigates the transmission mechanism and signal identification of power pulsation wireless communication. A three-dimensional full-scale fluid–structure coupling dynamic model incorporating the sucker rod, centering device, wellbore fluid, and tubing is established to characterize stress wave propagation from the downhole pump to the wellhead. The model reveals that the transmission channel exhibits typical high-impedance, low-pass characteristics, with fluid viscous damping, rod–tubing friction, and material damping governing signal attenuation, while low-frequency stress waves retain superior long-distance transmission capability. The model is validated using field-measured loading data, achieving prediction errors below 10% across the full operating condition range. Based on the validated model, a joint time- and frequency-domain identification algorithm is developed by combining characteristic spectral peak recognition with time-domain waveform verification, enabling detection of power pulsation signals under strong noise. The proposed model and identification method provide theoretical and technical support for wireless wellbore communication, downhole condition monitoring, and intelligent lifting systems, offering a reliable solution for real-time downhole informatio

title: Fractional Modeling of MHD Casson Flow with Heat and Mass Transfer in a Porous Medium Using the Constant-Proportional Caputo Derivative
abstract: In this study we developed a new model of fractional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) polymeric Casson flow, heat and mass transfer from a wall adjacent to a porous medium with viscous dissipation, heat generation and activation energy effects, a problem of relevance to non-Newtonian functional thermal materials processing and smart lubricant manufacturing.Fractional derivatives were used to extend the Casson viscoplastic model (which featured shear-thinning and yield stress effects) in order to represent complex non-Newtonian responses and memory-dependent behaviour.The mathematical formulation was developed using a newly suggested constant-proportional Caputo fractional derivative (CPCFD).The transformed dimensionless fractional governing equations for mass, momentum, energy and species concentration were solved via Laplace integral transform technique (LITT), under suitable boundary conditions.MATHCAD software was used to evaluate solutions for non-dimensional velocity, U temperature, T and concentration, C, with variation in transverse coordinate y and time t.Nusselt number, Sherwood number and skin friction solutions are also presented.The impact of key emerging parameters on these variables was examined.Verification with previous studies neglecting porous media, magnetic field, heat generation, activation energy and viscous heating effects is also included.An increase in activation energy parameter (E a ), i.e., minimum energy threshold required for a chemical reaction to occu

title: Fractional viscoelasticity in transient unentangled polymer networks
abstract: Stress relaxation in transient polymer networks often shows extended power-law behavior, G(t) ∼ t−β, where the exponent β frequently departs from the value 1/2 predicted by the sticky Rouse model and its variants. We introduce the fractional inhomogeneous Rouse model (FIRM), which uses a generalized Langevin equation driven by fractional Gaussian noise of exponent α, while retaining heterogeneous bead friction to represent sticky cross-links. Thus, FIRM unifies subdiffusive sticker dynamics and chain heterogeneity within a single framework. We show that the relaxation modulus G(t) can be represented as a linear combination of the squares of Mittag–Leffler functions. For homogeneous chains, it recovers two power-law regimes, t−α/2 and t−2α, on either side of the Rouse relaxation time. Fitting FIRM to stress relaxation data for an imine-based polystyrene vitrimer shows that α < 1 captures the shape of G(t) over finite observation windows. FIRM accommodates both Arrhenius and non-Arrhenius temperature dependences in the effective activation energy. We derive expressions for dynamic properties, such as mean-squared displacement and dielectric response, and outline how generalized memory kernels extend the framework to real materials. Together, these results suggest novel ways in which data from rheology, dielectric spectroscopy, scattering, and other experimental methods may be incorporated into a molecular model.

title: Current-driven Magnetic Skyrmions for Encoding/Storing Information: Manipulation and Dynamics in Nanoscale Structures
abstract: This dissertation investigates the dynamics of current-driven magnetic skyrmions, topological solitons in magnetic materials with broken spatial inversion symmetry, for low-power spintronic applications like racetrack memory and multilevel data storage. Skyrmions’ small size and low driving current requirements make them promising information carriers. The research examines skyrmion motion under driving currents, pinning effects, and thermal fluctuations, using numerical simulations (Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation), analytical studies (Thiele equation), and theoretical modeling to design novel data storage devices. The study analyzes skyrmion motion amidst pinning potentials from material imperfections. Simulations reveal that thermal fluctuations vary with damping: acting as a frictional force at low damping or a driving force aiding depinning at high damping. The Thiele equation quantifies this, though its accuracy wanes at low temperatures with pinning. The skyrmion Hall angle, influenced by current and pinning, provides insights for ambient-condition devices. These findings underpin a proposed multilevel data storage device, where controlled current positions skyrmions at pinning sites for high-density, low-power encoding. The research also explores altermagnetic (ATM) skyrmions, which exhibit d-wave symmetry via exchange-driven spin splitting. title: PROJECT GENESIS: QUANTUM TETRAHEDRAL HYBRID PROPULSION MANIFESTO GEN 1, PART 1: FOUNDATIONS OF BOUNDARY-LAYER FLUID DYNAMICS
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Project Genesis defines a scalable, multi-stage Quantum Tetrahedral Hybrid Propulsion System designed to achieve silent, high-efficiency, solid-state flight. This open-source architecture resolves the two critical limitations that have historically restricted atmospheric electrohydrodynamic (EHD) propulsion to lab-bench models: prohibitive energy requirements and extreme atmospheric sensitivity (arcing under high humidity). The system transitions past brute-force high-voltage scaling by establishing an integrated, multi-physics environmental loop. This spikes absolute air density and mass flow rate before the fluid encounters the primary positive ionic corona rings. title: Dismantling the “Commodity Trap”: Geopolitics, Value Chains, and Resource Nationalism in Africa and Ethiopia’s Critical Mineral Sector
abstract: This paper examines the structural architecture governing the extraction, processing, and trade of critical minerals within the contemporary global political economy. Using Dependency Theory (Frank, 1966; Amin, 1976) and the Resource Curse Paradigm (Auty, 1993; Sachs & Warner, 2001), we analyze the systemic core-periphery asymmetries that constrain developing countries to low-margin primary commodity extraction while consolidating high-value downstream refining and technological production in advanced industrial economies (Gereffi, 2014). We incorporate quantitative frameworks, specifically the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), to show how extreme consolidation in midstream processing functions as a strategic geopolitical choke point (IEA, 2023). Moving from global patterns to a specialized country assessment, this study investigates Ethiopia's nascent critical mineral sector. Focusing on the lithium-cesium-tantalum (LCT) pegmatites at Kenticha and the hydrogeological lithium-potash brine arrays of the Danakil Depression, we outline severe infrastructure deficits, extensive informal artisanal mining structures, and coordination friction between the Federal Ministry of Mines and Regional Mining Bureaus. Furthermore, we evaluate the distinct socio-economic vulnerabilities stemming from potential unrefined raw material flight, arguing that a failure to mandate localized refining locks the state into a permanent cycle of value leakage. title: MPM modelling of impact-loading shallow flow-like landslides in unsaturated slopes
abstract: Debris avalanches (DA) pose severe hazards in urbanized piedmont areas due to their large runout and potential for progressive volume increase through bed entrainment. Impact-loading mechanisms at bedrock outcrops can trigger cascading slope failures, yet the conditions controlling whether a small initial instability arrests or evolves into a catastrophic debris avalanche remain poorly understood.,This study proposes a hydro-mechanical framework for impact-induced debris avalanche inception, integrating an energy-based interpretation of the interaction between a moving saturated mass and a downslope unsaturated deposit. An advanced Material Point Method (MPM) model is developed to simulate the coupled evolution of stresses, pore water pressures, and deformations during the impact and afterwards. The simulations reproduce the loading exerted by the incoming mass and capture the progressive response of the impacted slope. Results show that the abrupt deceleration of the impacting mass leads to rapid pore pressure buildup in the impact zone and stress redistribution in successive downslope volumes. The evolution of kinetic energy reveals progressive energy transfer from the moving mass to the impacted soil, governing whether the instability is arrested or propagates downslope.,The parametric analysis demonstrates that initial soil suction in the impacted slope is the most important parameter controlling debris avalanche inception. title: Nonequilibrium Two‐Phase Wellbore Modeling of CO 2 Injection Shut‐In and Restart in Depleted Gas Reservoirs
abstract: ABSTRACT CO 2 injection into depleted gas reservoirs can operate close to the vapor–liquid equilibrium envelope because post‐depletion pore pressure is often much lower than in saline‐aquifer storage. This study applies a one‐dimensional transient two‐phase mixture solver with a Lee‐type evaporation–condensation source closure, hybrid Peng–Robinson/Span–Wagner CO 2 properties, transient radial heat transfer, and an injectivity‐coupled sandface boundary to a 1500‐m tapered‐completion CO 2 injector. The base case injects pure CO 2 at 30 kg/s into a depleted reservoir at 9.0 MPa. Three shut‐in durations (1, 10, and 30 min) and three restart durations (10, 30, and 60 min) are evaluated; selected shut‐in cases are benchmarked against RELAP5‐3D under matched conditions. The two solvers agree within approximately 1.7°C on the minimum wellhead temperature. Shut‐in collapses the frictional pressure contribution and leaves the upper wellbore below the local saturation pressure. The resulting vapor‐rich upper section absorbs latent heat and cools by more than 17°C in the upper 300 m. Modeled minimum wellhead temperatures range from −19.1°C for emergency shut‐in to −8.7°C for 30‐min controlled shut‐in. Restart can create a second flash‐cooling event; the 60‐min restart is not necessarily the thermally safest option because it prolongs the subsaturation flashing window. title: Predicted enhanced wear resistance and mechanical integrity in AA8011 composites via dual-ceramic ZrB2 and B4C reinforcement
abstract: The mechanical and dry-sliding wear characteristics of AA8011 aluminium matrix composites (AMCs) reinforced with 2, 4, 6 and 8 wt% zirconium diboride (ZrB₂) and boron carbide (B₄C) manufactured using the stir casting process at 760 °C and 380 rpm are explored. The microhardness, ultimate tensile strength (UTS), coefficient of friction (COF), and wear rate were systematically investigated as a function of reinforcement type, content and sliding distance. AAZ-8 composite showed that the microhardness was 93 HV, which is 34.78% higher than that of unreinforced AA8011 (69 HV), and ZrB₂ composite showed that its microhardness was 4.71–6.90% higher than AA8011/B₄C composite. The improvements in UTS were 42.2% and 45.5% for AAZ-8 and AA8011/8 wt% B₄C (AAB-8), respectively, when compared to AA8011 with UTS of 154 MPa. AA8011/8 wt% B₄C (AAB-8) resulted in 2.3–4.6% higher UTS than ZrB₂ at the same reinforcement concentration. The results of dry sliding tests with an EN31 steel counterface showed that the wear rate and COF decreased continuously as the reinforcement content increased and sliding distance carried out ranged from 600 m to 2400 m. The reasons for this improvement were attributed to improved load-bearing capacity, surface work hardening, debris redistribution and protective secondary tribological layers. title: Characterization and Stabilization of Collapsible Soils in Arid Regions Using Lime–Ceramic Waste Blends
abstract: ABSTRACT Collapsible soils, commonly found in arid and semi-arid regions, present significant geotechnical challenges: moisture induces collapse of their metastable structure, causing sudden settlement that jeopardizes infrastructure integrity. This study investigates the effectiveness of a composite binder consisting of 3 % lime and 4–8 % finely ground ceramic waste for stabilizing reconstituted collapsible soils representative of semi-arid and arid regions worldwide, using locally sourced North African materials. Specimens composed of 80 % Boussaâda sand and 20 % Djebel Debbagh kaolin were prepared, cured for 7 d under sealed conditions at 20°C ± 2°C, and evaluated using Atterberg limits, Standard Proctor compaction, one-dimensional oedometer flooding, and unconsolidated–undrained triaxial tests. Collapse potential, under one-dimensional oedometer flooding at 200 kPa, was reduced to less than 0.05 % at 8 % ceramic waste with 60-blow compaction energy, reclassifying the treated soil as non-collapsible. title: Editorial: The citizenship of international migrants: rethinking the migration–citizenship nexus today
abstract: Contemporary international migration has profoundly reshaped the social, political, and institutional landscapes of the twenty-first century. At the same time, citizenship-long regarded as a stable and territorially bounded institution-has become one of the most dynamic and contested concepts in public debate and academic research. Traditionally conceived as a formal legal status linking individuals to a nation-state, citizenship is today increasingly fragmented, stratified, and reconfigured by global mobility, heterogeneous legal frameworks, and new forms of socio-political inclusion and exclusion (Marshall, 1950;Soysal, 1994;Sassen, 2006;Shachar, 2009;Fauser, 2020;Strozza, Conti and Tucci, 2021;Trucco and Bargel, 2025). Migration has thus destabilized citizenship as a bounded legal status and recast it as a contested field of membership. This conceptual shift lies at the heart of critical theories of citizenship developed in dialogue with migration studies, which foreground citizenship as an enacted, relational, and claim-making practice rather than a fixed legal condition (Bloemraad, 2018;Isin and Nielsen, 2008). In this Editorial, we conceptualize the migrationcitizenship nexus as a critical analytical lens through which to understand these transformations. title: The Dynamic Analysis of the Passenger Car Steering and Braking Stability
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: During cornering-braking maneuvers, an excessively high braking torque can consume a substantial portion of the available tire-road friction and cause insufficient frictional capacity to satisfy the lateral force demand generated by cornering. As a result, the vehicle may experience stability degradation and, in severe cases, lose control, potentially causing accidents. In this study, an AMESim-based vehicle dynamics model is developed, and yaw rate and sideslip angle are adopted as the primary evaluation indices to characterize steering-braking behavior. Under conditions of a fixed turning radius and initial braking speed, the critical braking force was simulated and analyzed. Additionally, the critical steering wheel angle was examined under conditions of a fixed braking torque and steering speed. The results indicate that if either the braking force or the steering wheel angle exceeds its critical value, the vehicle will lose stability during combined steering and braking.

title: Hitch Position Sensitivity on Axle Loads and Braking Performance in Tractor-Trailers
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: The longitudinal dynamics during braking of articulated heavy vehicles is primarily governed by coupled load transfer mechanisms, yet the isolated influence of hitch location on axle load distribution and braking response remains insufficiently quantified. This study investigates the sensitivity of hitch height variation of a twin-axle tractor with a single-axle on the axle loads and consequently braking performance. A rigid-body longitudinal dynamics model is utilised and evaluated against a high-fidelity multibody simulation across a structured test matrix spanning friction levels and trailer loading conditions. Results show that hitch location primarily affects braking behaviour through redistribution of axle normal loads via hitch-induced pitching moments. A 400~mm increase in hitch height produces up to 5% variation in drive axle load in the unladen case, rising to approximately 16% under laden conditions. Longitudinal hitch variation yields comparable sensitivity in drive axle load, with increased influence on steer axle loading, while trailer axle load remains largely unaffected. Despite these variations, the overall braking metrics such as stopping distance and steady-state deceleration exhibit limited sensitivity to hitch location under most operating conditions. title: Modelling cornering speed in road cycling
abstract: Cornering performance is a key factor in downhill road cycling, yet the mechanisms governing speed regulation in turns remain poorly quantified. In this study, three professional cyclists performed repeated descents of a ~3 km road segment, with speed recorded at 10 Hz and turn geometry characterised through curvature. Minimum speeds in turns were found to be consistent across riders and primarily determined by the curvature radius R, with sharper turns leading to lower speeds. This behaviour is well described by a friction-based model vlim = (μ*g*R)1/2, which accurately predicts whether braking is required. A dynamical model incorporating this constraint reproduces the measured speed profiles and correctly identifies braking locations. These results demonstrate that a simple friction-based framework captures the main mechanisms governing speed regulation in downhill cycling and can be used to provide pre-race guidance on achievable speeds and appropriate precautions in each turn.

title: A system-level optimisation framework for marine diesel engine calibration and performance mapping
abstract: This study presents a sequential optimisation framework for marine diesel engine calibration and performance mapping. The framework couples a one-dimensional WAVE engine simulation model with a MATLAB-based nonlinear constrained optimiser, enabling systematic tuning of key control variables across the engine load diagram under realistic thermodynamic, operational, emissions, and combustion-stability constraints. The methodology is structured into three connected modules. The first module calibrates mechanical losses using an optimised friction model based on the Chen–Flynn correlation, ensuring accurate representation of friction mean effective pressure (FMEP). The second module calibrates nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions by tuning the Arrhenius coefficients of the extended Zeldovich mechanism. The third module embeds the calibrated friction and NOx submodels as fixed components within a system-level load-diagram optimisation framework. The optimisation adjusts turbocharger speed, fuel rate, start of injection, and injection duration while satisfying constraints on brake power, maximum pressure, maximum temperature, exhaust temperature, air–fuel ratio (AFR), NOx emissions, and combustion stability. AFR is used as a constrained air-management objective rather than as a direct surrogate for minimum brake-specific fuel consumption (BSFC). A BSFC-based constrained optimisation is also performed as a benchmark. The results demonstrate smooth, constraint-compliant, and physically co

title: Chapter 2: IoT-Enabled AI-Driven Energy Management and Optimization for Electric and Hybrid Vehicles
abstract: The concurrent proliferation of vehicular electrification and edge-connected telematics has fundamentally redefined the operational boundary conditions of automotive powertrain control. In modern electrified powertrains—encompassing pure Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs) with distributed multi-motor architectures and Plug-in Hybrid Electric Vehicles (PHEVs) featuring multi-mode power-split topologies—the supervisory Energy Management Strategy (EMS) governs the split between electrochemical and thermomechanical energy sources. However, real-world energy efficiency, battery longevity, and tailpipe emissions are heavily compromised when control decisions are made reactively without look-ahead environmental context. Traditional rule-based state machines, such as charge-depleting/charge-sustaining (CD-CS) heuristics, lack spatiotemporal foresight, resulting in premature battery depletion prior to high-load hill climbs and aggressive friction braking during sudden decelerations.

By maintaining bit-exact mathematical invariants across every node, the framework achieves absolute computational determinism and eliminates calculation drift. The codebase is built as a zero-dependency, sovereign stack structured across four core runtime modules: wad18.py (Fixed-Point Arithmetic Engine) for zero-drift integer calculations, r3.py (Russell Recursive Refinement) for formal symbolic logic validation, ledger.py (Immutable Cryptographic Audit Trail) for tamper-evident SHA-256 hash chains, and braking.py (Real-Time Safety & Actuator Control) for manag

title: Magnetohydrodynamic thermal analysis of Cu-Fe 3 O 4 /engine-oil hybrid nanofluid for thermal management in hydrogen energy systems
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part C Journal of Mechanical Engineering Science
abstract: Thermal management remains a critical challenge in contemporary energy and hydrogen-based energy systems, especially when considering fuel cells, hydrogen compressors, and compact heat exchangers in which high temperatures decrease efficiency and reliability. Motivated by the combined effects of thermophysical properties, non-Newtonian rheology, particulate contamination, porous resistance, and magnetic control, this study investigates MHD flow of an engine-oil-based Cu-Fe 3 O 4 hybrid nanofluid through an inclined porous channel. Cu enhances thermal transport, while Fe 3 O 4 enables magnetic control of the flow. The study considers an unsteady two-phase dusty Casson fluid model between inclined parallel plates under the influence of a relative magnetic field, taken to be fixed either with respect to the fluid (MFFRF) or with respect to the plate (MFFRP). Additionally, porous medium resistance, thermal radiation, and internal heat generation are incorporated to represent practical thermal systems. The governing momentum and energy equations are solved analytically using the Poincaré-Lighthill perturbation technique (PLPT). Thermal and flow characteristics are evaluated using engineering performance indicators, namely the skin-friction coefficient and the Nusselt number. From the results, it is observed that the heat transfer rate of the hybrid nanofluids is higher than that of the mono-nanofluids and conventional engine oil. title: Oxygenated nanoparticles influence on internal combustion (IC) engines performance, combustion, and emissions
publisher: Society for Structural Integrity and Life, Institute for Material Testing
abstract: One possible method to improve engine performance, optimise combustion properties, and lower hazardous emissions is the incorporation of oxygenated nanoparticles as fuel additives in internal combustion (IC) engines. These nanoparticles, typical metal oxides as Al2O3, CeO2, TiO2, and ZnO, enhance combustion through catalytic activity and serve as localised oxygen donors during fuel oxidation. Improved atomisation, quicker ignition, and higher heat release rates are all facilitated by their large surface area and thermal conductivity. According to experimental research, adding such nanoparticles to diesel, biodiesel, or mixed fuels at modest concentrations (usually 30-150 ppm) significantly increases brake thermal efficiency and decreases brake-specific fuel consumption. Due to complete combustion, emission measurements regularly demonstrate notable reductions in smoke, carbon monoxide, and unburned hydrocarbons. Nevertheless, higher in-cylinder temperatures and quicker flame propagation are frequently linked to a little rise in nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions. All things considered, the application of oxygenated nanoparticles presents a practical solution to enhance fuel efficiency and ecological sustainability in internal combustion engines, especially when combined with biodiesel plus exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) technology.

title: Performance, emissions, and predictive modelling of a CI-ICE operating in LPG–diesel dual-fuel mode
abstract: This study presents an experimental assessment of a compression-ignition internal combustion engine (CI-ICE) operating in dual-fuel mode with diesel and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), without fuel preheating or combustion enhancers. The objective is to evaluate the effect of LPG substitution on engine performance, emissions, and operational fuel costs under electric power generation conditions. Additionally, an artificial neural network (ANN) was developed using TensorFlow and Keras to capture relationships among key process variables at high altitudes; the model was trained on experimental data from the test campaign. Tests were conducted at several engine load conditions, comparing diesel operation with LPG–diesel dual-fuel blends, where diesel was partially substituted by LPG at three mass flow rates (0.18, 0.36, and 0.54 kg/h). Dual-fuel operation increased brake thermal efficiency by up to 10%, reaching 29.4% at 0.54 kg/h, while reducing brake specific fuel consumption. Specific emissions of CO and HC decreased significantly at medium and high loads, whereas NOx increased at full load. Fuel cost reductions reached 73% at full load. The ANN models achieved high predictive accuracy (R²>0.95), confirming their robustness for predicting CI-ICE performance in LPG–diesel dual-fuel mode. Therefore, ANN models provide a reliable tool for reducing experimental testing campaigns and associated operational and research costs. Finally, the findings confirm the technical feasibility

title: Experimental Investigation of the Effects of Hydrous Methanol (5% Water) on the Performance and Emissions of a Spark-Ignition Engine
journal: Journal of Modern Mechanical Engineering and Technology
abstract: Distillation is an inevitable step in the production of pure methanol to remove water and residual gases from its crude state. However, it increases the overall cost of production of concentrated methanol. The current study is targeted towards usage of hydrous methanol in an automotive spark ignition engine. Engine was run at stoichiometric equivalence ratio with a constant speed of 4000 rpm and variable torque (3-9 Nm). Water was blended in methanol by 5% v/v. The volumetric efficiency increased drastically with hydrous methanol by 22.5% and 14.7% at lower and higher torque respectively as compared to base methanol (100%). Brake thermal efficiency increased by 18% at lower torque and decreased by 21.6% at high torque with hydrous methanol. In addition to this, NOx emission decreased by 83.7% and 19.7% at lower and higher torque respectively with hydrous methanol. CO emission also decreased due to increase in air to fuel ratio with hydrous methanol.

title: Effects of Barium Carbonate and Barium Titanate Particle Additives on the Performance and Emissions of a Diesel Engine Fueled with an Olive Pomace Oil Biodiesel–Diesel Blend
abstract: Improving fuel efficiency while controlling exhaust emissions is important for the wider use of biodiesel blends. The effects of barium carbonate and barium titanate were compared using a base fuel composed of equal volumes of diesel and biodiesel derived from olive pomace oil. Each additive was evaluated at 25, 50, and 100 ppm, with diesel, untreated BP50, and neat biodiesel serving as reference fuels. Tests used a single-cylinder diesel engine operated at 2000 rpm over a brake power range of 1.0–3.0 kW. Performance, exhaust gas concentrations, smoke opacity, exhaust temperature, and sound pressure level were measured. For neat biodiesel, the largest increases relative to diesel were 24.52% in brake specific fuel consumption and 42.86% in nitrogen oxide concentration. At 2.0 kW, the formulations containing 50 ppm BaCO3 and BaTiO3 exhibited brake specific fuel consumption values 3.80% and 3.79% below that of BP50, respectively. Both formulations raised brake thermal efficiency from approximately 22.38% to 23.27%. Relative to BP50, maximum reductions were 44.32% in carbon monoxide concentration with 50 ppm BaTiO3 at 2.5 kW, 40.00% in hydrocarbon concentration with 100 ppm BaCO3 at 2.5 kW, and 31.25% in smoke opacity with 50 ppm BaCO3 at 1.0 kW. However, NOX concentrations increased by up to 19.87% with 100 ppm BaTiO3 at 2.0 kW compared with BP50. title: Hybrid Quantum-Photon Propulsion for Interstellar Flight: Mathematical Analysis and Comparative Assessment (2026–2050)
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract. This paper presents a rigorous mathematical analysis of interstellar propulsion architectures for near-term missions (2026–2050). We demonstrate that classical solar and laser sail concepts, including Breakthrough Starshot and thermonuclear-track proposals, suffer from insurmountable physical contradictions: diffraction-limited beam divergence, energy gigantomania, relativistic erosion, and the fatal absence of autonomous braking. We then analyze quantum photon engines based on the dynamic Casimir effect (DCE), showing that pure DCE propulsion requires either external energy infrastructure or onboard reaction mass that collapses mission efficiency. We propose and mathematically substantiate a hybrid propulsion architecture combining interstellar medium (ISM) particle capture with proton-catalyzed vacuum emission in MOF (metal-organic framework) metamaterial resonators. Quantitative mission modeling for a 3-ton post-biological starship carrying 10 modified anthropomorphic agents to Proxima b yields achievable cruise velocities of 0.1c–0.5c, flight times of 13–50 years, and total ISM fuel consumption of 0.3–3 kg over the entire mission. We conclude with a formal comparative proof that, within the technological horizon 2026–2050, the hybrid architecture is the only physically and logistically viable path to crewed interstellar flight.

title: SonoDyno: A Sonic Dynamometer for Engine Speed and Load Estimation from Audio
abstract: Controllable engine sound synthesis, Active Sound Design and engine order analysis all build on the relationship between the sound of an engine and its momentary operating state: its speed and its load. Recordings of engine sound are abundant in archives, sample packs and online video, yet they rarely carry time-aligned annotations of that state, which limits their applicability to controllable engine sound generation. We present SonoDyno, which estimates the engine speed, the cylinder count and an engine-normalized load intensity from a microphone signal alone, with no tachometer, no bus access and no prior knowledge of the engine configuration. A convolutional scorer of 124,302 parameters reads the harmonic order energy of each frame at three time-frequency resolutions to jointly score cylinder count and speed, and a decoder imposes the rotational dynamics of the engine on the speed trajectory. A second head estimates the load intensity, the position of the torque between the engine's drag floor at 0 and its full-load ceiling at 1, from the order levels at the decoded speed. On recordings of engines it has never heard, with microphone position, engine type and cylinder count unknown, SonoDyno places 93 to 97% of the frames within 2% of the true speed, identifies the cylinder count with 80% accuracy and confuses the octave on fewer than 2% of the frames.
